Anatomy of Urinary System
Anatomy of urinary system
Kidney
• The kidneys are bilateral bean-shaped organs
• Located retroperitoneally (behind the peritoneum) in the abdomen, 
either side of the vertebral column.
• They typically extend from T12 to L3, although the right kidney is 
often situated slightly lower due to the presence of the liver.
• Each kidney is approximately three vertebrae in length.
• The adrenal glands/suprarenal glands (Glandula Suprarenalis) 
located superiorly to the kidneys within the renal fascia
Anatomical Position
Anatomical Position
Kidney Structure
The kidneys are encased in complex layers of 
fascia and fat. They are arranged as follows 
(deep to superficial):
1.
Renal capsule (capsula fibrosa) – Tough 
fibrous capsule.
2.
Perirenal fat (Capsula Adiposa) – Collection 
of extraperitoneal fat.
3.
Renal fascia (Fascia renalis) – Encloses the 
kidneys and the suprarenal glands.
4.
Pararenal fat – Mainly located on the 
posterolateral aspect of the kidney.
• The renal parenchyma is 
composed of  Cortex renalis and 
medulla renalis. 
• The cortex extends into the 
medulla, dividing it into 
triangular shapes – these are 
known as renal pyramids 
(Pyramida renalis).
• The apex of a renal pyramid is 
called a renal papilla. 
Internal Structure of Kidney
• Each renal papilla is associated 
with a structure known as 
the minor calyx, which collects 
urine from the pyramids. 
• Several minor calices merge to 
form a major calyx
• Urine passes through the major 
calices into the renal pelvis, a 
flattened and funnel-shaped 
structure (berbentuk corong). 
• The medial margin of each 
kidney is marked by a deep 
fissure, known as the renal 
hilum. 
• Hilum acts as a gateway to the 
kidney 
• The renal vessels and ureter 
enter/exit the kidney via this 
structure.
Vasculature
• The kidneys are supplied with 
blood via the renal arteries (Arteri
Renalis), which arise directly from 
the abdominal aorta
• The right renal artery (A. Renalis
Dextra) is longer, and crosses the 
vena cava posteriorly.
• A. Renalis is located in the distal 
of A. Mesenterica Superior
• Each renal artery enters the 
kidney via the renal hilum, 
dividing into segmental 
branches. 
• These branches are :
1.
A. Renalis polaris Superior
2.
A. Renalis anterior; A. Renalis
anterior superior and A. Renalis
anterior inferior
3.
A. Renalis posterior
4.
A. Renalis polaris inferior
Vascular renal segments
Venous Drainage
• The kidneys are drained of 
venous blood by the left and 
right renal veins (Vena Renalis). 
• They leave the renal hilum 
anteriorly to the renal arteries, 
and empty directly into the 
inferior vena cava.
• The left renal vein is longer, and 
travels anteriorly to the 
abdominal aorta. 
Adrenal glands/Glandulae suprarenalis
• Endocrine gland that produce 
steroid hormones
• The adrenal gland consists of 
cortex and medulla
• Located in the superior of the 
kidney
• It’s not the part of Urinary 
system
Ureter
• Ureters are two thick tube of 
smooth muscle with 25 cm 
long
Parts of ureter :
• Pars abdominalis: in the 
retroperitoneal space
• Pars pelvica: in the lesser 
pelvis
• Pars intramuralis: traverses 
the wall of the urinary bladder
Ureter
Constriction :
• The exit from the renal 
pelvis
• The crossing of the A 
iliaca communis or A. 
iliaca axterna
• The passage through the 
wall of the urinary 
bladder (most narrow) 
Dorsal view
ventral view
Vesica Urinaria
• The urinary bladder/Vesica urinaria is located in the 
subperitoneal space
• Composed of : Corpus vesicae, apex vesicae and fundus 
vesicae
• The Ostium urethrae internum and the two Ostium ureteris
form the trigonum vesicae at the fundus vesicae
• The vesical urinaria is positioned directly superior to the 
prostate gland. 
Urethra
• The urethra opened ventrally
• There are 4 parts of urethra :
1. Pars-intramuralis
2. Pars-Prostatica
3. Pars-membranacea
4. Pars Spongiosa
Anatomy of Male Reproductive system
Learning Objective
Anatomy of The Male Reproductive system
•
Scrotum
•
Testis and epydidimis
•
Ductus Deferens and Glands
•
Urethra and Penis
Scrotum
• The scrotum is a fibromuscular cutaneous sac, located 
between the penis and anus. 
• Embryologically, the scrotum is derived from the genital 
swellings 
• In the adult this fusion is marked by the scrotal raphe. 
• The scrotum is biologically homologous to the labia majora.
Scrotum
The scrotum contains three major structures:
• Testis – the site of sperm production.
• Epididymis – situated at the head of each testicle. It functions as 
a storage reservoir for sperm.
• Spermatic cord – a collection of muscle fibres, vessels, nerves 
and ducts that run to and from the testes.
• Dartos muscle is a sheet of smooth muscle, situated immediately 
underneath the skin. It acts to help regulate the temperature of 
the scrotum, by wrinkling the skin – this decreases surface area, 
reducing heat loss.
Scrotum
Neurovascular supply 
• The scrotum receives arterial supply from the anterior and posterior 
scrotal arteries.
• The anterior scrotal artery arises from the external pudendal artery, 
while the posterior is derived from the internal pudendal artery.
Cutaneous innervation to the scrotum
• Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve – Supplies the anterolateral 
aspect of the scrotum.
• Anterior scrotal nerves – Supplies the anterior aspect of the scrotum.
• Posterior scrotal nerves – Supplies the posterior aspect of the 
scrotum.
• Perineal branches of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve – Supplies 
the inferior aspect of the scrotum.
The Testes and Epididymis
• The testes have an ellipsoid shape.
• The testes consist of a series of lobules, each containing seminiferous 
tubules supported by interstitial tissue.
• The testes have two coverings. 
• The tunica vaginalis is situated externally, covering the anterior 
surface and sides of each testicle.
• The tunica albuginea is a fibrous capsule that encloses the testes. It 
penetrates into the parenchyma of each testicle, dividing it into 
lobules.
The epididymis consists of a single heavily coiled duct and can be 
divided into three parts; 
• Head – The most proximal part of the epididymis. It is formed by the 
efferent tubules of the testes, which transport sperm from the testes 
to the epididymis.
• Body – Formed by the heavily coiled duct of the epididymis.
• Tail – The most distal part of the epididymis. It marks the origin of the 
vas deferens, which transports sperm to the urethra for ejaculation.
Epidydimis
The Testes and Epididymis
Vas deferens
• Vas deferens is duct that transports sperm from the epididymis to the 
ejaculatory ducts, ready for ejaculation
• The wall of the vas deferens contains a smooth muscle consists of 
three muscle layers – inner layer of longitudinal muscle, intermediate 
layer of circular muscle, and an outer layer of longitudinal muscle
• Autonomic innervation of these muscle fibres permits fast movement 
of sperm towards the ejaculatory duct
The anatomical course of 
the vas deferens
• It is continuous with the tail of 
the epididymis.
• Travels through the inguinal 
canal.
• Moves down the lateral pelvic 
wall in close proximity to the 
ischial spine.
• Turns medially to pass between 
the bladder and the ureter.
• Joins the duct from the seminal 
vesicle to form the ejaculatory 
duct.
Prostate Gland
• The prostate is the largest accessory gland in the male reproductive 
system.
• The prostate is commonly described as being the size of a pingpong
ball
• The prostate is positioned inferiorly to the neck of the bladder and 
superiorly to the external urethral sphincter
• Posteriorly to the prostate lies the ampulla of the rectum
Normal and enlarged of prostate gland
Prostate Gland
• The prostate is the largest accessory gland in the male reproductive 
system.
• The prostate is commonly described as being the size of a pingpong
ball
• The prostate is positioned inferiorly to the neck of the bladder and 
superiorly to the external urethral sphincter
• Posteriorly to the prostate lies the ampulla of the rectum
Penis
The penis is an external organ of the male reproductive system. It has 
two main functions:
• Sexual intercourse – The penis undergoes erection, becoming 
engorged with blood. Following emission, (mixing of the components 
of semen in the prostatic urethra) ejaculation can occur, whereby 
semen moves out of the urethra through the external urethral orifice. 
Finally, the penis undergoes remission, returning to a flaccid state.
• Micturition – The penis also has an important urinary role. It contains 
the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder to the external 
urethral orifice, where it is expelled from the body.
Structure of the Penis
The penis can be anatomically divided 
into three parts:
• Root : The most proximal, fixed part of 
the penis. 
• Body : The free part of the penis. It is 
composed of three cylinders of 
erectile tissue – two corpus 
cavernosa, and the corpus 
spongiosum.
• Glans : The most distal part , and is 
formed by the distal expansion of the 
corpus spongiosum
External structure of Penis
External structure of Penis

2. Sulcus coronaries 
glandis
3. Corona glandis
4. Glans penis

externum
6. Frenulum preputii
7. Corpus penis
